newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Institute sees grim outlook for Yugoslav economy.
newsitem.headline: Institute sees grim outlook for Yugoslav economy.

text.p: The Yugoslav economy is on the verge of collapse and the government is facing stark economic options -- recession or rampant inflation, the Belgrade-based Institute of Economic Sciences said on Tuesday.

The Yugoslav economy, hit by a shortage of working capital, a $2.26 billion trade gap in 1996, growing public spending deficit, increasing pressure for wage rises and no fresh funds in sight, is on the verge of collapse, it said.
The funds are blocked by an entire range of political and economic prerequisites set by the West for the country's return to the world's financial organisations, it said.
The West has made any return to bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) conditional on political as well as economic change by the socialist government.

"The only prospect for Yugoslav economy prior to its full reintegration into the world is recession whose length and scale depends on the possibilites to urgently secure funds to revive the production and finance the existing trade gap," the institute's director Tomislav Popovic told reporters.
The gloomy picture of the economy cannot be changed by adjusting statistical methodology or by hiding some data from the public, the institute warned in its latest monthly report.

The downward trend in industrial output which began last November continued in January by dropping 20.8 percent against December. Year-on-year change was 2.9 percent up according to the adjusted methodology.
"January output would have been between 3.5 to four percent below the January 1996 level if the old methodology was applied," said the Institute's leading economist Stojan Stamenkovic.
Retail prices continued to stabilise with a 1.4 percent rise in January and only 0.6 percent in February.
January exports stood at $132.4 million, up 42.7 percent against the same month in 1996 but down 21 percent against last December.
Imports stood at $322.7 million, up 39.7 percent against January 1996 but 18.5 percent down against December.
Trade gap of $190.3 million was up 37.8 percent against last January but narrowed by 16.8 percent against December.
"This was expected due to already exhausted funds of non-defined origin abroad that have financed the 1996 trade gap of $2.2 billion," Stamenkovic said.
The government collected a record low of 2.74 billion dinars for its state coffers in January, or 1.1 billion less in nominal figures than in December.
"In real terms this is a record low since January 1995," Stamenkovic said.
After strong monetary expansion in December and a plunge in the dinar black market rate, the central bank restored stability of the dinar by sopping up 262 million dinars.
It also decreased money in circulation to 48 percent in January against 54 percent in December, Stamenkovic said.
"The stability of the dinar and prices was maintained by the restrictive monetary policy," he said.
This has adversely affected the cash-starved economy and resulted in stagnating production and deepening recession," Stamenkovic said.
"Easing monetary control with change in prices and exchange rate would stimulate the production but will reignite inflation in the long run," he said.
